title: Early-Life Famine Exposure and Risk of Cardiovascular Diseases in Later Life: Findings From the REACTION Study.
ehr_evidence: We used data from REACTION (Risk Evaluation of Cancers in Chinese Diabetic Individuals: A Longitudinal) Study, which recruited a total of 259 657 community-dwelling adults aged 40 years or older from 25 centers across mainland China between 2011 and 2012.
summary: Observational study examining the association between early-life exposure to the Chinese famine (1959-1962) and the risk of cardiovascular diseases in adulthood among a large Chinese cohort.
key_findings: Fetal famine exposure was associated with increased risk of total CVD (OR 1.35, 95% CI 1.20–1.52), MI (OR 1.59, 95% CI 1.08–2.35), stroke (OR 1.40, 95% CI 1.11–1.78), and CHD (OR 1.44, 95% CI 1.26–1.65).

Childhood famine exposure was associated with increased risk of total CVD (OR 1.59, 95% CI 1.40–1.81), MI (OR 2.20, 95% CI 1.52–3.20), stroke (OR 1.82, 95% CI 1.45–2.28), and CHD (OR 1.80, 95% CI 1.56–2.09).

Adolescent famine exposure was associated with increased risk of total CVD (OR 1.52, 95% CI 1.27–1.81), MI (OR 2.07, 95% CI 1.28–3.35), stroke (OR 1.92, 95% CI 1.42–2.58), and CHD (OR 1.83, 95% CI 1.50–2.24).
Individuals in severely affected famine areas had significantly increased risk of total CVD compared to those in less severely affected areas across all exposure groups.
The association between early-life famine exposure and CVD risk was stronger in women, non-smokers, non-drinkers, and those without moderate-to-vigorous physical activity.
Part of the impact of famine exposure on CVD was mediated via metabolic syndrome.
captured_features: lifestyle factors (smoking, drinking, physical activity, diet)
anthropometric measurements (height, weight, BMI, waist circumference)
serum lipids (total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, triglycerides)
study_design: cross-sectional analysis of baseline cohort data
population: 234,219 community-dwelling Chinese adults aged 40 years or older from 25 centers across mainland China
limitations: misclassification bias due to defining exposure by birth date
famine severity index based on excess death rate did not account for other causes of mortality
self-reported cardiovascular disease leading to recall bias
cross-sectional design precludes assessment of CVD incidence and mortality
